claims.text: High configurational entropy retards elemental segregation in nanoalloys at high temperature.
High configurational entropy retards phase separation in nanoalloys at high temperature.
The retardation of segregation and phase separation occurs because configurational entropy raises diffusion activation barriers.
High configurational entropy promotes formation of a thin, uniform, self-passivating oxide layer.
The thin oxide layer impedes further oxidation and chemical degradation.
The high-entropy alloy nanoparticles initially have a homogeneous elemental distribution.
Chemical disorder exists across grain boundaries and within the nanoparticle core.
Individual-element diffusion is slower in the high-entropy nanoalloy because its diffusion activation barriers are elevated.
Compared with binary or lower-entropy analogues, high-entropy nanoalloys will exhibit slower oxidation kinetics at high temperature.
Compared with binary or lower-entropy analogues, high-entropy nanoalloys will exhibit less phase separation at high temperature.
Slower oxidation and reduced phase separation will allow high-entropy nanoalloys to maintain greater structural and chemical stability.
The prediction is expected to apply around 900 °C in atmospheres with limited oxygen.
Under extremely oxidizing conditions, degradation mechanisms other than entropy-mediated diffusion retardation and passivation may dominate.
At temperatures near the alloy melting point, other degradation mechanisms may dominate.
A controlled comparison should expose high-entropy and binary or low-entropy nanoparticles to 900 °C with trace oxygen for the same fixed period.
Phase evolution, oxidation kinetics, oxide thickness, and elemental redistribution are the proposed measurable responses.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant reduction in both oxidation kinetics and phase separation relative to the control would falsify the hypothesis.
